# ConStore: Search-Overlapped Prefetch and Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Storage for Disk-Based ANNS

### Abstract

Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) supports retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search, recommendation, and advertising over corpora that exceed memory capacity. Existing ANNS research often focuses on vector search at small top-_K_, whereas industrial-scale applications require larger retrieval sets. Fetching the corresponding content from storage remains comparatively unexplored. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector corpora shows that, at large _K_, content fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency and cannot be ignored in end-to-end retrieval.

We present ConStore, a content storage engine combining two complementary techniques to reduce end-to-end retrieval latency. Speculative Inline Content Prefetch (SICP) commonly abstracts graph-based and cluster-based ANNS as progressive SSD I/O that refines an in-flight candidate queue. It prefetches content for stable leading candidates under a bounded I/O budget, overlapping content reads with search without changing the final top-_K_ results. Co-Retrieval- Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG) uses query logs to place frequently co-retrieved documents in contiguous segments. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) adapts this layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget. Group Content Fetch (GCF) exploits this layout to coalesce per-document random reads into batched, page-aware I/O requests. SICP works independently of the content layout, while RPAG and GCF reduce fetch cost even without prefetching.

Across three multi-hop QA workloads with _K_ from 10 to 1600, ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency over the best per-document-read baseline by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN. Separate experiments on 100M- and billion-vector indexes demonstrate SICP’s applicability at larger scales.

### 1 Introduction

Disk-based approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) has been widely adopted to overcome the memory limitations of large-scale vector search [6, 19, 46]. By keeping large indexes on SSD rather than entirely in DRAM, these systems support retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search,

recommendation, and advertising over corpora containing millions to billions of vectors [19, 32].

Once a query is embedded, the storage-facing ANNS retrieval pipeline has two phases: _vector search_ identifies the top-_K_ item IDs, and _content fetch_ loads their associated payloads from storage for downstream processing. For example, RAG loads passages for an LLM prompt, while search and recommendation retrieve item content or features for re-ranking and presentation. Both phases contribute to end- to-end retrieval latency.

Prior work has heavily optimized vector search through two main families of disk-based indexes. Graph-based systems, including DiskANN, PipeANN, OdinANN, and Starling, optimize graph traversal, storage layout, or update handling [13, 14, 46, 52]. Clustering-based systems, including SPANN and FusionANNS, organize vectors into clusters for efficient candidate retrieval [6, 48]. In contrast, the content- fetch phase that delivers the selected payloads has received comparatively little attention.

Much ANNS research emphasizes small top-_K_ settings such as _K_=10, but industrial applications retrieve hundreds or thousands of candidates. Recent study reports search workloads with _K_ around 100-3,000 to supply downstream re-ranking models and advertising workloads with _K_ up to 3,000 [19]. These larger retrieval sets challenge the assumption that content fetch is only a minor overhead. Our profiling across million- to billion-vector indexes shows that content-fetch latency can match or exceed vector-search latency at large _K_ (Figures 2 and 3). At small _K_, vector search pays an initial cost to locate promising regions of the index. As _K_ grows, expanding and scoring the candidate set adds work, while fetching fixed-size payloads requires proportionally more content reads. In the measured large-_K_ regime, both phases exhibit approximately linear growth with _K_, making content fetch a first-class retrieval cost rather than a negligible follow-up.

Conventional retrieval serializes content fetch after vector search, waiting for the final top-_K_ IDs before issuing content reads. We study graph-based and clustering-based ANNS and it reveals a shared opportunity: both can be viewed as _progressive SSD I/O processes that iteratively refine a candidate queue_. DiskANN reads graph neighborhoods, while SPANN

reads and scores posting lists in batches. In both cases, likely results emerge before search finishes, allowing some content reads to overlap with the remaining search I/O.

Choosing when and what to prefetch is non-trivial. Early candidates can change, wasting content reads; late prefetches leave too little search time to hide their cost. Variable search tails and competition for SSD bandwidth therefore require selective, budgeted speculation.

Another challenge is that content is commonly stored in insertion or key order, unrelated to which items are retrieved together [38, 51, 53]. Co-retrieved payloads are consequently scattered, requiring many random reads and limiting opportunities for coalescing.

Embedding-based clustering is an imperfect alternative: proximity in vector space need not imply co-access. A multi- hop query can retrieve a film page and its director’s biography from different semantic clusters. Grouping content by observed co-retrieval patterns can capture this locality that insertion order and embedding clusters miss.

We present ConStore, a content storage engine for disk- based ANNS that reduces end-to-end retrieval latency through two complementary techniques: overlapping content fetch with search and reducing fetch cost through co-retrieval-aware layout. Either technique can be deployed independently. Our contributions are:

1. Content-fetch profiling: Across million- to billion-vector indexes, we show that content-fetch cost grows approximately linearly with _K_ and can match or exceed vector- search latency, motivating optimization of the complete search-plus-fetch pipeline.<tbc>

2. Speculative Inline Content Prefetch (SICP): Using the shared progressive-I/O abstraction, SICP prefetches content for stable leading candidates under a bounded I/O budget and fetches missing payloads after search. It preserves the final top-_K_ and requires only a document-to- extent lookup, independent of content layout.<tbc>

3. Co-Retrieval Content Segments (CCS) with Group Content Fetch (GCF): Retrieval-Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG) uses query logs to group frequently co-retrieved documents into contiguous CCS segments. At query time, GCF coalesces requested content into batched, page-aware reads. Together they reduce fetch cost without changing the ANN engine, with or without SICP. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) adapts the layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget when recurring co-retrieval patterns change.<tbc>

4. Evaluation: On three multi-hop QA workloads, ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN over the best per-document- read baseline, while preserving retrieval results. Ablations isolate each technique, and synthetic-payload experiments<tbc>

on 100M- and billion-vector indexes demonstrate SICP at larger scales.

## 2 Background and Motivation

### 2.1 ANNS Retrieval Pipeline

ANNS-based applications that consume retrieved payloads have two coupled storage phases: vector search and content fetch. The vector-search phase probes an ANN index to identify the top-_K_ item IDs; the content-fetch phase loads the associated text, item content, or features from a content store. In the conventional pipeline, these reads begin after search returns its final IDs. Content fetch therefore adds its own storage I/O to end-to-end retrieval latency rather than being part of the vector-search operation.

ANNS supports more than RAG: semantic search retrieves candidate documents [27, 29], recommendation and advertising retrieve items for downstream ranking or filtering [19], and visual similarity search retrieves related images [26]. In RAG, retrieved passages supply external knowledge to an LLM [32, 50].

### 2.2 Disk-Based ANN Indexes

Disk-based ANN indexes are used because billion-scale vector corpora cannot keep all full-precision vectors and search metadata in DRAM at reasonable cost. Modern disk-based ANN systems mainly fall into two families. The first is graph-based search, including DiskANN, PipeANN, OdinANN, and Starling [13, 14, 46, 52]. DiskANN keeps a compact in-memory structure, such as entry points and compressed vectors, while storing full-precision vectors and graph neighborhoods on SSD. Query processing performs a beam search over the graph: each hop reads a batch of candidate neighbors from SSD, scores the newly loaded vectors, updates the candidate queue, and issues the next batch of graph reads. Thus the top-_K_ result is refined over multiple SSD-I/O rounds rather than being produced by a single blocking lookup.

<tbc>The second family is clustering-based, IVF-style search, represented by SPANN and extended by systems such as FusionANNS and Helmsman [6, 19, 48]. SPANN uses an in-memory head index to route a query to nearby clusters, while the vectors inside each cluster are stored as posting lists on SSD. The refinement phase reads selected posting lists progressively, often one list or a small internal batch at a time, scores their vectors, and merges them into the current result buffer. Its progress signal is therefore posting- list completion rather than graph-hop completion.

## 2.3 Motivations and Challenges

Much ANNS research focuses on small top-_K_, such as _K_=10, where content fetch can be a relatively small part of retrieval latency. Industrial workloads often need larger candidate sets: Helmsman reports search _K_ around 100-3,000 for re- ranking and advertising _K_ up to 3,000 [19]. Our profiling shows that content fetch can match or exceed vector-search latency at large _K_, challenging the assumption that search always dominates the retrieval pipeline.

Vector-search latency depends on both index size _N_ and result count _K_. At small _K_, navigation to promising regions can dominate search time. As _K_ grows, candidate expansion and scoring add work, while fetching fixed-size payloads requires proportionally more content reads. Figures 2 and 3 show this trend from small- to large-scale indexes: in the measured large-_K_ regime, both phases grow approximately linearly with _K_, making content fetch non-negligible.

**Parallel post-search fetch is not enough.** Parallel payload reads after search can reduce an isolated query’s fetch latency, but they leave the two phases still serialized with T\_search + T\_fetch. Under concurrent serving, one query’s burst of content reads competes for SSD bandwidth and queue capacity with other queries’ graph or posting-list reads. Uncontrolled parallelism can therefore inflate search latency rather than remove the bottleneck.

**Overlap content fetch with vector search.** Despite their different index structures, DiskANN and SPANN expose the same opportunity: progressive SSD I/O refines a candidate queue before the final top-_K_ is known. The key insight is that the head of this queue can stabilize early, allowing likely result payloads to be prefetched while search continues rather than waiting for it to finish.

Designing an effective prefetch mechanism is non-trivial. Prefetching too early wastes bandwidth because the candidate queue is still unstable; prefetching too late leaves too little search tail to hide content I/O. The right trigger also depends on _K_, query difficulty, and the selected ANN backend, because each changes both candidate stability and remaining search time. A useful mechanism must expose enough overlap to matter while bounding wasted reads and leaving time for final top-_K_ verification plus any residual content fetch.

Embedding-based clustering is only a proxy for co- retrieval locality. A question about a film director’s birthplace may need both the film page and the director’s biography, even if their embeddings lie in different clusters. Such documents benefit from co-location based on observed co-access rather than embedding proximity alone.

## 3 ConStore Overview

ConStore reduces end-to-end retrieval latency by overlapping content reads with vector search and reducing the I/O required to fetch content. Prefetching exploits available SSD bandwidth during search under a bounded I/O budget; layout optimization reduces content-I/O demand.

The two techniques are complementary and independently applicable (Figure 4). First, SICP (§4) prefetches likely result payloads from the evolving ANN candidate queue, overlapping reads with search while preserving the final top-_K_. It works with any content layout that provides a document-to-extent lookup.

Second, co-retrieval-aware layout with grouped fetch (§5) reduces per-fetch cost. RPAG groups frequently co-retrieved documents into CCS segments, and GCF coalesces requested content into page-aware reads. Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR, §5.3) adapts this layout to workload shifts by selectively regrouping segments under a bounded rewrite budget when recurring co-retrieval patterns change. This path requires no ANN-engine changes and benefits both prefetching and post-search fetch.

1 separates _when_ reads execute from _how much I/O_ they require. Combined, SICP issues GCF’s grouped reads during search, sharing the same planner with post-search fetch.

**_Lifetime of a query._** While the foreground ANN search runs, one background worker observes read-only candidate snapshots and prefetches through GCF when stability and budget checks pass. Search runs to completion with its final top-_K_ unchanged. ConStore then joins the worker and fetches any missing result payloads through the same GCF path.

§4 first presents SICP, the more general of the two techniques; §5 then formalizes the storage and layout primitives that make each fetched window cheaper.

## 4 Speculative Inline Content Prefetch

Prefetching must balance early candidate churn against a shrinking search tail. SICP exploits the key insight that leading candidates can stabilize before the full search completes: it checks read-only _candidate snapshots_, admits a bounded set of likely results, and overlaps their page-aware content reads with search. Repeated small prefetches adapt to later candidates without committing the entire budget to an early snapshot. A post-search _residual fetch_ serves any final top- _K_ documents not covered by speculation, preserving the search results and recall. The mechanism requires only a document-to-extent lookup, so it works with both insertion- order payload files and the layout of §5.

§4.1 presents the overall design, §4.2 develops the policy that decides when each prefetch starts and which content windows it admits, and §4.3 describes the engine-level hooks that expose search progress.

### 4.1 Overall Design

Figure 5 shows the SICP process and contrasts it with the sequential baseline. SICP performs one full ANN search, but instruments the existing DiskANN/SPANN search loop with a lightweight read-only progress callback. Each callback reports how far the search has advanced and copies the current ranked candidate state into a candidate snapshot. For DiskANN, progress is measured in graph-search hops; for SPANN, progress is measured by SSD posting-list entries processed during refinement. A background _prefetch worker_ consumes these snapshots and issues content reads; it cannot modify, prune, or reorder the foreground vector search.

Before issuing a prefetch, the worker applies the stability and progress checks of §4.2 to avoid spending bandwidth on transient candidates. It admits only a bounded number of new candidates, skipping documents covered by earlier<tbc>

To reduce I/O requests, a page-aware planner maps selected document IDs to content extents and coalesces nearby extents into page-aligned read windows. In ConStore this planner is GCF (§5.4); over an insertion-order payload file, where co-retrieved documents rarely share pages, it degenerates to one aligned window per document. The worker records scheduled documents and windows so later prefetches and the residual fetch do not repeat the same work.

The foreground search is unchanged and continues to its natural completion. It does not observe prefetch decisions, so it returns the same final top-_K_ as a non-instrumented run. After search returns, SICP computes the residual demand: final top-_K_ documents that are not already covered by prefetch. This residual fetch can run while the prefetch worker finishes outstanding work, and it avoids documents already scheduled by prefetch so the same content is not fetched twice. If speculation misses, the remaining final documents are fetched normally. Figure 6 walks through these steps for one query.

**Bounded I/O overhead.** SICP bounds speculative work at three levels: the number of prefetches, the maximum documents admitted per prefetch, and the per-prefetch I/O budget. It also tracks what previous prefetches have already selected, so a candidate that remains near the head of the queue is not planned repeatedly. The extra I/O beyond the sequential baseline is limited to windows for speculative candidates that do not survive into the final top-_K_; final documents that were not prefetched are still served by the residual path.

For one prefetch, the ideal wall-clock saving is bounded by min(_T_prefetch\_io, _T_search\_tail), where _search\_tail_ is the remaining vector-search time after the prefetch is issued and _prefetch\_io_ is the worker’s content-I/O time for that prefetch. With multiple prefetches, the same accounting applies repeatedly: content I/O completed before the search returns is removed from the foreground fetch path, while any worker wait or residual fetch remains visible.

## 4.2 Prefetching Strategy

The strategy answers two questions continuously throughout the search: _when_ should the next prefetch start, and _what_ additional content should it fetch? A simple all-or-nothing trigger - fire once and prefetch the whole current top-\(K'\) - is brittle. It overcommits when the remaining search tail is short, and it cannot react when later callbacks promote new documents into the head of the queue. SICP instead treats the search tail as a series of small budgets. Each prefetch spends only a bounded amount of I/O, deduplicates against previous prefetches, and leaves all misses to the residual fetch. The strategy has three components.

**(1) Progress and stability checks - when to fire.** These checks reduce wasted reads from early candidate churn while retaining time to overlap useful I/O. At every progress callback, the prefetch worker considers issuing a prefetch only if the callback is new and the per-query prefetch cap has not been reached. The first check is progress: DiskANN must have completed enough hops, and SPANN must have processed enough SSD posting-list entries. The second check is candidate stability. SICP compares the ranked top-\(K'\) document set against the previous check using set-overlap similarity. After the head remains stable for a configured number of checks, the worker may fire. A late-progress threshold prevents pathological waiting when the search tail is almost gone. Later prefetches reuse the same checks but also require a minimum number of newly promoted documents, so SICP does not issue a prefetch for a tiny or duplicate delta.

**(2) Budgeted page-aware prefetch - what to fetch.** Budgeting limits speculative device pressure, while coalescing reduces the requests needed to fetch selected candidates. When prefetching, the prefetch worker ranks the current candidate snapshot and forms a bounded pool: at most \(K\cdot\alpha\) documents, further capped by a per-prefetch maximum. Documents already selected by earlier prefetches are excluded. The remaining candidates are passed to a budgeted selector, which chooses a prefix under the prefetch I/O budget. The first prefetch can size its budget from the estimated remaining search tail. Subsequent prefetches use a small per-prefetch budget so that the worker continues to track the queue as it evolves, rather than spending the entire budget on one early snapshot. SICP keeps a compact coverage record for scheduled and completed content windows, so later prefetches avoid both document-level duplicates and page-level duplicates caused by adjacent documents sharing the same content page.

**(3) Residual content fetch - handling misses.** The residual path ensures complete final results even when speculation misses, without duplicating pending reads. After vector search returns, the final top-_K_ is authoritative. SICP subtracts all documents covered by completed prefetch reads. It also treats documents scheduled by an in-flight prefetch as pending, so the foreground path does not immediately duplicate the same content work. The foreground then fetches the remaining final documents with the same page-aware planner while the prefetch worker finishes outstanding work.

### 4.3 Per-Engine Instrumentation

Each engine provides a read-only callback that publishes candidate snapshots and a progress counter to the shared prefetch worker. The callback leaves search logic unchanged and requires no suspension or restart.

**DiskANN.** On-disk beam search advances through graph- search hops, reading candidate neighborhoods from SSD and refining the candidate queue. An optional callback at configurable hop intervals publishes the current queue and hop counter. The background worker uses successive snapshots to check stability and select bounded content reads, allowing multiple prefetches as candidates evolve. The callback does not modify the queue or traversal; the foreground search continues to completion.

**SPANN.** An in-memory head search selects candidate posting lists, which are read from SSD and scored to refine the result buffer. We instrument this refinement loop to publish capped, sorted candidate snapshots at configurable posting-count intervals. The processed-posting count supplies the progress signal in place of DiskANN’s hop counter, letting the same worker apply stability checks and budgeted prefetching. Head-index navigation, posting-list selection, and foreground refinement remain unchanged, preserving the final top-_K_.

## 5 Co-Retrieval-Aware Content Layout and Group Fetch

SICP (§4) hides content I/O behind the search tail but does not change how much I/O each fetch costs: with an insertion- order payload store, every prefetched or residual document is still a separate random read. This section presents the<tbc>

<tbc>second, independent technique of ConStore, which reduces the per-fetch cost itself. It consists of an on-disk segment format (CCS, §5.1), an offline co-retrieval-aware layout policy (RPAG, §5.2), and an online grouped, page-aware fetch path (GCF, §5.4). The three are used by the post-search fetch path on their own, and by SICP’s prefetch worker when the two techniques are combined.

### 5.1 Co-Retrieval Content Segments (CCS)

A _Co-Retrieval Content Segment_ (CCS) stores a bounded group of documents contiguously in the order chosen by the layout policy. Grouping by co-retrieval rather than embedding proximity lets jointly requested documents share content reads, reducing random I/O even when their embeddings are far apart. The offset-addressed format comprises a fixed-size metadata header, a per-document index of (_offset_, _length_) pairs, and a contiguous content block. Embeddings, graph edges, and posting lists remain in the ANN engine’s index, keeping content placement independent of the search backend.

Offsets support direct lookup of individual payloads. When requested documents share a segment, GCF (§5.4) reads their index slab once and coalesces their extents into page-aware windows. Both post-search fetch and SICP use this path to exploit the locality created by RPAG (§5.2).

ConStore maintains a single doc\_map that resolves any document ID to its segment and local index in _O_(1). The runtime representation is a packed pair of 32-bit integers, so the map costs 8 B per document, roughly one percent of the embedding-side ANN index memory in our workloads. This small fixed metadata cost keeps the fetch path independent of the ANN engine while avoiding a per-query hash lookup or external metadata lookup on the critical path.

### 5.2 Co-Retrieval-Pattern-Aware Grouping (RPAG)

The effectiveness of CCS depends critically on which documents share a segment. Documents grouped together pay one batched page-aware read plan per top-_K_ overlap; documents in different segments require separate segment-level plans. The layout policy is therefore the lever that controls the per-fetch-cost axis of  1.

**Co-retrieval graph and partition objective.** RPAG treats the training retrieval log as a weak supervision signal for physical locality. Each document is a vertex in a graph _G_=(_V,E_). For a query _q_, let _R<sub>q</sub>_ be the ANN result list and \(\rho_q(d)\) be the rank of document _d_ in that list. For every pair of documents that co-occur in _R<sub>q</sub>_, RPAG adds an undirected edge whose contribution depends on the worse rank of the pair. For wider training lists, RPAG can avoid treating all top-_K_ co-occurrences equally by using prefix-weighted edges: pairs that co-occur in the head of the result list receive the largest weight, and pairs that co-occur only in deeper prefixes receive progressively smaller weight. RPAG instantiates this rule with an ordered prefix set \(\mathcal{C}=\{\kappa_1<\cdots<\kappa_L=K\}\) and<tbc>

monotonically decreasing weights \(\alpha_1>\cdots>\alpha_L\): \(w_{uv}=\sum_{q:u,v\in R_q}\alpha_{\ell(q,u,v)},\)
\(\ell(q,u,v)=min\{\ell:max(\rho_q(u),\rho_q(v))\le\kappa_\ell\}.\) This weighting makes the segment layout reflect the documents most likely to be requested together by the retriever, while still retaining weaker evidence from the tail of a wider result list. For multi-round retrieval traces, edges are added both within a round and across adjacent rounds, capturing the locality needed by iterative RAG queries. The partitioning goal is to group documents so that high- weight edges stay inside a bounded CCS segment: \(max_{\{S_i\}}\sum_l\sum_{(u,v)\in E,u,v\in S_i}w_{uv}\text{s.t.}|S_i|\le B.\) This is balanced graph partitioning [28] and admits direct off-the-shelf solvers. RPAG partitions each connected component of the co-retrieval graph; small components become segments directly, while larger components are split by METIS into roughly equal-sized parts. The result is a document- to-segment assignment that the CCS writer materializes as segment files and a packed doc\_map. Because the objective mentions only document IDs and query co-occurrence, it is independent of the ANN engine that will later produce those IDs. A pure co-retrieval graph covers only documents observed in the training log. Treating unobserved documents as arbitrary isolated vertices would make their placement unstable and would waste segment capacity on weak evidence. Con- Store therefore uses a hybrid assignment: documents with sufficient co-retrieval support are placed by RPAG, while cold or unseen documents inherit an embedding k-means placement. This fallback is not a separate online path; it is resolved once when the CCS files are written, so every query still uses the same constant-time doc-id-to-segment lookup. **Page-aware intra-segment refinement.** Segment membership decides which documents can be fetched together; the order inside a segment decides whether those documents share the same SSD pages. We therefore apply a page-aware refinement, RPAG, after the hybrid RPAG/k-means assignment. RPAG preserves each segment’s document set and constructs a second co-retrieval graph only among documents already assigned to that segment. It uses the same prefix-weighted evidence as above inside each existing segment, but now the objective is linear ordering rather than partitioning: co-retrieved documents should appear near each other in the segment’s content block so that GCF can cover them with one or a few page-aligned read windows. For each touched segment, RPAG greedily packs the intra- segment graph. It starts from the document with the largest weighted degree, then repeatedly appends the strongest unplaced neighbor of the current document; when a connected component is exhausted, it resumes from the highest-degree remaining document. The CCS writer then rewrites the segment’s content bytes and local id order according to this permutation, leaving untouched segments byte-identical. This step does not change recall or segment membership: it only converts the locality that RPAG exposes at segment granularity into page locality that the page-aware GCF planner can consume. ## 5.3 Workload-Adaptive Segment Reorganization (WASR) RPAG’s layout can become stale when queries begin retrieving different documents together. We propose _Workload- Adaptive Segment Reorganization_ (WASR) to adapt the layout to these workload shifts. A background controller regroups selected segments only when recurring co-retrieval patterns reveal degraded locality and the expected I/O savings justify rewriting them. Queries continue using the constant-time doc\_map of their current layout version while reorganization runs. **Learning recurring locality.** Real workloads often exhibit skewed popularity, with popular queries and entities revisited. A learned layout benefits only when document pairs are retrieved together again. WASR measures _pair recurrence rt_: the fraction of epoch _t_’s co-retrieval edge weight contributed by pairs seen in earlier epochs. It retains k-means placement without confirmed co-retrieval evidence and avoids rewriting for unpredictable workloads. **Online co-retrieval monitor.** The monitor identifies recurring pairs while aging out obsolete evidence. It samples completed queries’ _final_ top-_K_ lists, not provisional ANN candidates, and aggregates each epoch of _E_ queries into a time bucket. Bucket rotation expires old evidence. The monitor also keeps the undecayed occurrence count _n<sub>t</sub>(u,v_) over these buckets; a pair is _confirmed_ when \(n_t(u,v)\ge\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the minimum repeat count. This filters one-off co-occurrences before they can trigger rewrites.

**Layout-quality signal and trigger.** To avoid rewriting for frequency changes that do not harm locality, WASR tracks the _confirmed cut ratio_ of assignment _P_, where _P(u_) is document _u_’s segment:

\(\chi_t(P)=\frac{\sum_{(u,v):n_t\ge\theta,P(u)\neq P(v)}w_t(u,v)}{\sum_{(u,v):n_t\ge\theta} w_t(u,v)},\)

Otherwise, WASR compares \(\chi_t\) with the reference \(\chi^*\) recorded at layout publication. Planning requires a rise greater than \(\delta\) for _h_ consecutive epochs and recurrence \(r_t\ge r_\mathrm{min}\). Here \(\delta\) is the tolerated degradation, _h_ filters transient shifts, and _r_<sub>min</sub> requires repeated evidence. A plan must also clear the gain threshold below, avoiding rewrites with little expected benefit.

**Budgeted bundle planning.** WASR reorganizes bundles of whole segments to preserve balanced groups and page locality without leaving partially dead segments. The planner charges each confirmed cross-segment edge to both endpoints’ segments, ranks segments by cut weight per byte, and selects them with their heaviest cut partners under a byte budget. Joint selection lets newly co-retrieved documents be regrouped. METIS repartitions the bundle into segments of at most _B_ documents, followed by RPAG’s intra-segment ordering; documents without recent edges retain their previous grouping, packed first-fit. A plan is accepted only if the recovered cut weight is at least a fraction _g_<sub>min</sub> of total confirmed weight.

A token bucket adds _b_ times the corpus bytes per epoch and caps accumulated credit, bounding rewrite volume and bursts after quiet periods. Foreground queue-depth and tail- latency guardrails further limit the active rewrite rate.

**Immuitable generations and reclamation.** To keep queries consistent during reorganization, each layout generation contains segment files and its own doc\_map. Publication writes new segments under fresh IDs, hard-links untouched files, records a manifest, fsyncs, and atomically renames the staging directory. Each query pins one generation, so it never mixes old and new layouts; the ANN index and recall remain unchanged. Retired segments are deleted only after the last reader of the old generation exits. Replacing whole segments avoids holes and garbage collection within partially live files.

### 5.4 Group Content Fetch (GCF)

GCF is the runtime mechanism that consumes the locality created by CCS and RPAG. For each query, ConStore uses the document-to-segment map and per-document content index described in §5.1 to collect requested documents that fall in the same CCS segment. The segment is the planning scope, but the read unit is a page-aware content window rather than the whole segment.

Within a segment, GCF turns the requested documents into a small window-planning problem. It first orders the requested local document IDs, reads the corresponding contiguous content-index slab, and converts each (_offset, length_) entry into an absolute file extent. Alignment is performed on these absolute offsets, so the planned windows correspond to the device pages actually read rather than to offsets relative to the segment’s content block.

To reduce requests without excessive overfetch, GCF scans extents in offset order and greedily merges their page-aligned windows. A merge that adds no pages is always accepted; otherwise it must satisfy caps on window size, read amplification (aligned bytes divided by useful bytes), and the gap between extents. If a cap fails, the planner starts a new window; a single large document still receives a complete aligned window. Nearby requested content thus shares I/O, while distant content is fetched separately rather than reading the whole segment.

The same window plan is used by both SICP’s prefetch worker and the post-search residual fetch. After a planned window is issued, documents whose content ranges are fully covered by fetched pages are marked warm, allowing the residual path to skip them and fetch only uncovered final top-_K_ documents. This bookkeeping does not change the ANN result or the window-building rule; it only shares page coverage between the speculative and residual uses of GCF.

The result is fewer content read requests and fewer device pages per top-_K_ fetch. A GCF hit amortizes the segment’s content-index access and serves multiple co-retrieved documents from one shared window; a miss simply degenerates to the normal single-document window. This lowers IOPS demand and queueing pressure without changing ANN search results or depending on a particular ANN backend.

## 6 Evaluation

### 6.1 Setup

Experiments run on a two-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230N server with 2.30 GHz 40 cores, 251 GiB DRAM and a 1.6 TB Intel SSDPEDME016T4 NVMe SSD.

**Datasets.** The primary corpus is Wikipedia DPR [27], with 21M passages averaging 1 KB and 768-dimensional embeddings. We use three multi-hop QA workloads: 2WikiMultihopQA [18], HotpotQA [57], and MuSiQue [49], containing 12,576, 7,405, and 2,417 questions, respectively. Each<tbc>

measured question comprises two retrieval hops; we report paired hop1+hop2 latency. Scaling experiments use SIFT100M and SIFT1B from BIGANN [23], with synthetic 1KB payloads.

**RPAG layout construction.** For CCS segments built with RPAG, we use a K-prefix co-retrieval objective that uses cumulative top-_K_ prefixes at \(K\in\{10,20,40,80\}\) with weights 1.0, 0.3, 0.1, and 0.03, respectively. This gives lower-_K_ co- retrieval pairs more influence during partitioning and intra- segment ordering, prioritizing the more latency-sensitive small-_K_ cases while still retaining signal from larger retrieval sets.

**ANN engines.** Our ANN engines are DiskANN[46] and SPANN[6]. DiskANN is a graph-based SSD ANN engine: compact vector summaries stay in memory, while graph and data pages are served from SSD; we set the search width _L_ per _K_ (68-1600 for _K_=10-1600) for recall@_K_≈0.90 which is a common recall target in evaluation practice of related work [6, 13, 14, 19, 46, 48]. For SPANN we set SearchInternalResultNum per _K_ (110-1152 for _K_=10- 1600) for recall@_K_≈0.90 and issue posting-list reads in batches of 8. Together, these two engines cover graph-based and cluster-based SSD retrieval, and ConStore uses their returned document IDs plus engine-specific candidate hooks for SICP (§4.3). We select these representative backends to

evaluate both index families, rather than compare all search- engine variants. PipeANN optimizes DiskANN-style graph traversal, while OdinANN extends this line to maintain stable performance under updates [13, 14]; we do not evaluate them here. Faster vector search makes unchanged content fetch a larger fraction of retrieval latency, strengthening the motivation to optimize it, but can also shorten SICP’s overlap window. We bounded bandwidth of vector search of SPANN to simulate production concurrent environments.

**Baselines.** We compare against three baselines. (1) Seq\_ Random stores content in a single binary file under a random corpus insertion order and fetches results via per-document I/O request. Insertion-order payload storage follows current production practice [38, 51]. (2) Seq\_KMeans stores content in CCS segments organized by embedding K-Means, testing semantic co-location without co-retrieval-aware grouping. (3) Seq\_RPAG stores document content in CCS segments organized by RPAG and uses the same GCF-batched fetch path as ConStore, but fetches content only after ANN search completes. SICP-only adds speculative prefetch to the Random layout; ConStore combines prefetch with RPAG and GCF. These variants separate overlap from layout benefits while preserving the final top-_K_.

## 6.2 End-to-End Retrieval Latency

Figures 8 and 9 show that most savings come from reducing or overlapping foreground content fetch, while search time changes little. The callback only publishes candidate snapshots; stability checks and page selection run on the background worker, limiting search-side overhead.

Seq\_RPAG isolates the layout benefit: relative to Seq\_ KMeans, it reduces latency by up to 18% on DiskANN and 9% on SPANN, although a few SPANN settings regress by up to 2%. The DiskANN benefit peaks near the largest trained prefix and declines beyond it. This is consistent with RPAG concentrating locality on the co-retrieval patterns represented in its training objective, rather than embedding proximity alone.

ConStore adds SICP to hide part of the remaining fetch behind search. Across per-dataset settings, it reduces end- to-end latency over the best per-document-read baseline by 4-48% on DiskANN and up to 25% on SPANN. Benefits generally grow with _K_ as more content I/O becomes available to overlap; small-_K_ SPANN cases show little benefit. The SICP-only ablation confirms that prefetching benefits even the Random layout. On DiskANN, layout alone is faster at smaller _K_, while prefetch alone becomes more effective at large _K_. Combining both gives the lowest geometric-mean latency at every evaluated _K_ on both engines: grouping reduces the work, and speculation hides part of what remains.

## 6.3 Prefetch Precision and Coverage

We evaluate SICP’s prefetch quality on the RPAG layout used by ConStore in Figures 8 and 9.

Figure 10 shows that many selected candidates survive into the final results: precision is 62.6-98.3% for DiskANN and 70.4-99.9% for SPANN. Both cover over 99% of results at _K_=160.

## 6.4 Scalability

Figure 11 compares ConStore with Seq\_KMeans and Seq\_ RPAG as concurrency grows from one to 32 queries. ConStore retains the lowest latency on both engines. Its single<tbc>

<tbc>search thread per query only publishes snapshots; the worker overlaps bounded content reads with search. RPAG and GCF reduce the content-I/O demand that would otherwise compete with concurrent searches.

Figure 12 compares ConStore with Post-Parallel-Fetch, which parallelizes content reads only after search. Under a 100ms total-P99 SLO and a 95% achieved/offered-QPS gate, ConStore increases sustainable offered QPS by 20% on DiskANN and 12.5% on SPANN. At the baselines’ highest sustainable rates , P99 latency is lower by factors of 1.46\(\times\) and 2.90\(\times\).

Both engines therefore sustain higher load before saturation: bounded search-fetch overlap reduces exposed fetch time without enough added contention to erase the benefit.

### 6.5 Scaling with Top-_K_ and Index Size

We evaluate SICP on SIFT100M and SIFT1B at recall targets 0.90, 0.95, and 0.99. Sequential fetches the synthetic payloads after search; SICP overlaps reads from the same insertion- order file.

Figure 14 shows that overlap remains useful at both scales without changing the final top-_K_. At recall targets 0.90/0.95, DiskANN’s latency reductions reach 42% on SIFT100M and 40% on SIFT1B; SPANN saves 30-43% at _K_=1600 across the two scales. The gain depends on the search/fetch balance, not scale alone: at SPANN’s 0.99 target, search dominates and the corresponding savings fall to 6-11%. Thus, larger result sets create more work to overlap, but a search-dominated pipeline limits the relative end-to-end benefit.

### 6.6 Content Fetch Speedup

We now turn to the second technique and isolate the layout side, measuring content fetch after search completes with no prefetch involved.

**Page-aware fetch and local ordering.** Figure 15 compares Serial (no page-aware coalescing), Page-aware planner (same layout, aligned coalesced reads), and PA + RPAG local reorder (intra-segment reordering followed by the planner). Planning helps both K-Means and RPAG; reordering further places co-retrieved documents on nearby pages, making each read more useful. With both optimizations, RPAG lowers fetch latency by 45-47% over Random and 19-22% over K-Means using the same optimized fetch path. The advantage therefore comes from co-retrieval locality as well as the shared planner.

**Cross-hop reuse opportunity.** RPAG places about half of hop-2 results in segments touched by hop-1, versus roughly 15% for K-Means and 4% for Random ( 2). Grouping co-retrieved evidence thus creates reuse opportunities across hops on both engines. This is a layout-derived upper bound, not a measured cache-hit rate: hop-1 may read only some pages of a segment, and actual reuse requires those pages to remain cached.

### 6.7 Layout Staleness and Adaptation

We replay the DiskANN hop traces as a chronological stream of 500-query epochs under a zipfian query popularity. Four warm-up epochs build the initial layout; each later epoch is evaluated before its queries reach the monitor. For example, "WASR 0.5%" adds rewrite allowance equal to 0.5% of corpus bytes each epoch. Unused allowance accumulates in a capped token bucket, so a single reorganization can exceed one epoch’s allowance; rewrites occur only when the adaptation checks in §5.3 pass. Benefit retention is (_L_<sub>kmeans</sub>-<tbc>

<tbc>_L_<tbc>

<tbc>)/(_L_<sub>kmeans</sub>-_L_<sub>oracle</sub>), where _L_ is the mean number of segments touched per two-hop query under the evaluated policy, and _L_<sub>kmeans</sub> and _L_<sub>oracle</sub> are the corresponding means for K- Means and the oracle. These quantities measure segment accesses, not latency. The oracle is a full rebuild that knows the confirmed graph of the next four epochs.

Figure 16(a) shows that static RPAG loses its locality advantage after the workload shift. WASR detects the degradation and restores locality through selective reorganization: with a 1% per-epoch budget, it rewrites 10.8% of the corpus in total, versus 25% for periodic full rebuilds. Targeting affected segments thus adapts the layout with substantially less rewriting.

Across the seven scenarios in Figure 16(b), WASR rewrites 2.5-12% of the corpus, compared with 15-26% for periodic full rebuilds. Its recurrence and gain checks focus this budget on shifts with reusable co-retrieval patterns rather than rebuilding on a fixed schedule. On the unique-query replay, WASR avoids rewriting entirely because there is insufficient recurring evidence, while periodic rebuilds still incur rewrite cost.

## 7 Related Work

**Vector search optimization.** A long line of ANN work reduces the cost of candidate generation through compression, graph navigation, filtering, and specialized hardware execution. FAISS, product quantization, optimized product quantization, ScaNN, HNSW, and NSG improve vector representation or in-memory search efficiency [8, 11, 15, 22, 26, 35]. DiskANN and SPANN move billion-scale search to SSDs; Filtered-DiskANN, FreshDiskANN, SPFresh, Starling, and FusionANNS extend this line with filters, updates, disk-layout optimization, or CPU/GPU execution [6, 12, 45, 46, 48, 52, 55]. ANN benchmarking work characterizes the recall/latency tradeoff of such indexes [3]. These systems optimize Phase 1 search I/O or scoring; they do not optimize Phase 2 content fetch.

**Retrieval and RAG models.** Neural retrieval systems such as REALM, DPR, RAG, FiD, RETRO, and Atlas show that generation quality depends on retrieving external evidence, often at large _K_ or over very large corpora [5, 17, 20, 21, 27, 32]. More recent active, self-reflective, corrective, and interleaved retrieval methods make retrieval part of the generation loop [2, 10, 24, 50, 56]. Dense and late-interaction retrievers such as ColBERT, ColBERTv2, and PLAID further improve retrieval quality and efficiency, while BEIR and Natural Questions broaden retrieval evaluation [29, 30, 42, 43, 47]. These works motivate larger and repeated evidence fetches, but they do not change how retrieved payloads are placed on storage.

**RAG and LLM serving systems.** RAGCache, Mooncake, and RAGO optimize RAG serving through KV-cache reuse,<tbc>

<tbc>disaggregated KV-cache management, or pipeline scheduling \[25, 39, 54\]. General LLM serving systems such as Orca, vLLM, SGLang, FlexGen, DistServe, Sarathi-Serve, Splitwise, and ZERO-Infinity improve batching, memory management, offloading, or phase disaggregation for model execution \[1, 31, 37, 40, 44, 58-60\]. They optimize the LLM side of the pipeline; ConStore optimizes the storage-side content path that feeds the prompt.

**Storage for AI workloads.** Recent AI-storage systems tailor data formats and runtime scheduling to ML workloads. ServerlessLLM introduces loading-optimized checkpoint formats, FlacIO reduces I/O amplification for ML artifacts, and CacheLib provides a production DRAM/SSD caching engine for object workloads \[4, 9, 34, 61\]. These systems share ConStore’s workload-aware philosophy, but they target model loading, container or artifact I/O, and caching rather than the co-retrieval layout of RAG content.

**Vector DB payload storage.** Classic storage systems such as LFS, LSM-trees, RocksDB, and WiscKey optimize write- optimized layout, compaction, or key-value separation for general storage workloads \[7, 33, 36, 41\]. Production vector databases adopt practical payload stores: Milvus and MANU use binlog/object-store style layouts, Qdrant replaced RocksDB with Gridstore, and Weaviate uses a custom LSM \[16, 38, 51, 53\]. These systems store payloads by insertion order, key order, or segment format; none use co-retrieval- aware layout or implement GCF-style batching.

## 8 Conclusion

ConStore treats content fetch as a first-class cost of disk- based ANNS retrieval. SICP overlaps bounded content reads with search, while RPAG and GCF reduce fetch I/O through co-retrieval-aware layout. The techniques are complementary and preserve the final top-_K_; together, they reduce end- to-end retrieval latency by up to 48% on DiskANN and 25% on SPANN over the best per-document-read baseline.
